transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hello. I suppose what made me come in is that my eating has just gotten all turned around lately. Some days I just forget lunch completely. I'll be sitting there watching out the front window—the Robinsons across the street just painted their front door this bright, awful red color, and I was watching the painters tape it off, wondering why on earth anyone would choose red for a brown brick house. It clashes terribly, don't you think? It's just an eyesore. 

But anyway... other days, I don't know, I just stand right at the kitchen counter eating crackers and sweets. Just standing there mindlessly. And the funny thing is, nothing even tastes right. I bought those little buttery crackers that were on sale at the grocery store on Tuesday, the ones in the yellow box, but they just taste like cardboard to me now. I don't know why I even buy them if they're just going to taste like that. The cashier there, the young girl with the glasses, she always bags my groceries too heavy anyway... but yes, my eating is just all out of sorts.
How have your mood and spirits been lately?

Well, my spirits... I suppose they haven't been very good. Most mornings I wake up with this terrible heavy, low feeling. It's just like all the color has drained right out of the day before I even put my slippers on. I bought those slippers at that little discount shop downtown, you know the one near the old post office? They're a lovely pale blue, but the soles are already wearing thin. They just don't make things the way they used to. My husband, rest his soul, used to have a pair of leather ones that lasted him fifteen years. Fifteen years! Now you buy something and it falls apart in a month. It's just a shame. But yes, I just feel so low when I wake up, just sitting on the edge of the bed looking at those blue slippers, wondering how I'll get through the morning.
Have you ever experienced a period in your life before where you felt this low?

Well, no, I don't think I've ever felt quite this heavy before. Not that I can remember, anyway. I've always been a fairly steady person, you know? Even when things were difficult, like when they decided to reroute the bus line right past my bedroom window. Oh, the noise from those buses! They used to run down Elm Street, which made perfect sense because it's wider, but then they had that whole city council meeting—I didn't go, of course, because it was pouring rain that night and my umbrella had a broken spoke. I meant to take it to the repair shop, but the man who used to fix umbrellas retired and moved to Florida. His daughter still lives here, though, she works at the bank. But anyway, no, I've never felt this low in my life. It's just a very strange, heavy feeling.
Have you ever had a time in your life when you felt the opposite—unusually energetic, elated, or on top of the world, needing very little sleep?

Energetic? Oh, heavens no. I've never been the type to bounce off the walls or anything like that. I've always needed a good eight hours of sleep, at the very least. If I don't get my rest, I'm just no good to anyone. 

Speaking of rest, I actually bought one of those memory foam mattresses a while back to try and help with my sleep. Well, I say a while, it was probably around the time my sister's dog had that litter of puppies. Golden retrievers... oh, they were precious little things, but they chewed through absolutely everything. She had this beautiful antique rug in her front hallway, passed down from our mother, and one of those puppies just tore the fringe right off one side of it. My sister was beside herself. She tried to have it repaired, but the man at the carpet shop said the weave was too old to match the thread. It's a shame, really, how nice things just get ruined like that. 

But yes, the mattress... the salesman told me it would be wonderful for my lower back. He was a very tall man, kept adjusting his tie the whole time he talked to me. I think his collar was too tight, he looked terribly uncomfortable. But no, I don't think I've ever felt on top of the world or gone without sleep like you're saying. I just like to get my rest.
Have you noticed any problems with your memory or confusion lately?

Well, my mind does get awfully foggy lately. Just the other day, I was sitting at the kitchen table trying to decide if I should call the pharmacy about my heart pills or open the mail first. I just sat there staring at the envelopes. The top one had a stamp with a little bluebird on it, which reminded me of the bird feeder my husband built. He used this lovely cedar wood—smelled wonderful—and he hung it right outside the kitchen window so I could watch the cardinals while I washed the dishes. We used to get so many cardinals back then. Now it's mostly just those pesky squirrels stealing all the seeds. I tried putting cayenne pepper in the birdseed because someone at the grocery store told me birds can't taste it but squirrels hate it. The cashier, a nice girl named Brenda, she's the one who told me. She always wears these brightly colored headbands. Anyway, I sat there staring at the mail and the phone, and my thoughts were just so muddled and slow that I ended up doing neither. I just left the mail right there on the table next to the salt shaker.

Well, it's been quite a while now. I'd say this low, colorless stretch has been with me for about a year and two months. It started right around the time the leaves started changing color last autumn. I remember because I was trying to knit a scarf for my niece, Emily. She was moving up to Chicago for a new job—something in marketing, I think. Or maybe it was public relations. She always was such a talkative girl, even when she was little. She'd sit on my living room rug and just chatter away to her dolls for hours. 

Anyway, I was knitting her this lovely mustard-yellow scarf because it gets so terribly windy up there by the lake. I had bought the yarn from that little craft shop on Main Street, the one with the creaky wooden floors. The owner, Mrs. Higgins, she makes the most wonderful spiced cider during the holidays. She always keeps a slow cooker full of it right by the register. It smells like cinnamon and cloves the second you walk in. But I just couldn't finish that scarf. My hands felt so heavy, and I just didn't have the heart for it anymore. I ended up putting it in a basket in the closet, and it's been sitting there ever since. So yes, about a year and two months of feeling like this.
Have you had difficulty taking care of your daily responsibilities, like managing your medications, paying bills, or preparing your own meals?

Well, I suppose I do put off things that used to just be part of my normal routine. I actually stopped teaching my craft classes down at the community center because of it. We used to have such a lovely time. Last spring we were doing decoupage... taking those pretty paper napkins and pasting them onto glass jars to make lanterns. My friend Martha brought in these beautiful napkins with little hydrangeas on them. Hydrangeas are so temperamental to grow, though. I tried planting them in my front yard years ago, but the soil here is just too alkaline. They turned this muddy pink color instead of that brilliant blue. My neighbor told me you have to add coffee grounds to the dirt to get the blue, but my husband didn't drink coffee, only tea, so we never had any grounds. Lipton, usually, with just a little squeeze of lemon. 

Anyway, I haven't been back to teach in months. And I've been missing phone calls and appointments, and all sorts of family tasks I used to handle so carefully. Like my nephew's birthday... I completely forgot to call him. I remember when he was born, it was the hottest July on record. The hospital air conditioning broke down, and they had to bring in these massive yellow fans that sounded like airplane engines. It was miserable for his poor mother. 

But yes, I still manage to stay in my home, thankfully. I haven't had to move in with anyone. I just have to rely a lot more on reminders now... little sticky notes on the fridge and the counter, otherwise I just put everything off and nothing gets done.
Have you ever gotten lost or confused about where you were while walking or driving in familiar places, like your own neighborhood?

No, I can't say I've ever gotten lost like that. I've lived in this neighborhood for... oh, it must be forty years now. We bought the house right after the big blizzard of '78. I remember the snow was piled so high you couldn't even see the mailboxes. We had to shovel a path just to get to the street, and my husband's shovel actually snapped in half because the ice was so thick underneath. He had to borrow one from Mr. Henderson next door. Mr. Henderson was such a nice man, he used to grow the most enormous tomatoes I've ever seen. Beefsteaks, he called them. He'd bring us a basket every August, and I'd make these wonderful tomato sandwiches on white bread with just a little mayonnaise and salt. You can't get tomatoes that taste like that at the supermarket anymore. They always taste so mealy and watery, like they've been sitting in a refrigerator for weeks. I tried growing my own once, in a little pot on the back porch, but the squirrels got to them before they even turned red. Those squirrels just take one bite out of a green tomato and leave it sitting on the railing. It's so frustrating. But no, I always know my way around the streets here.

I used to love getting the mail, you know. Back when people actually wrote letters. I wore that sweater until the elbows gave out. I tried to patch them with some leather ovals, but my sewing machine kept jamming. It was an old Singer that belonged to my mother, one of those heavy black ones with the gold filigree. It weighed a ton. final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for a major depressive episode (F32), characterized by a persistent low and heavy mood, marked anhedonia and loss of taste, fatigue, and cognitive slowing ('foggy' thinking and indecisiveness) lasting for 14 months. This is her first such episode, and she denies any past manic or hypomanic symptoms. Her cognitive complaints began after the onset of the depressive mood and are consistent with depressive pseudodementia rather than a primary neurocognitive disorder.

confirmed_symptoms: Persistent low, heavy mood upon waking with a feeling that all color has drained from the day
Loss of interest and pleasure in previously enjoyed activities (stopped teaching craft classes, abandoned knitting)
Alteration in appetite and loss of taste (food tastes like cardboard, mindless snacking and skipping meals)
Impaired concentration, slow thinking, and marked indecisiveness

additional_requirements: No lifetime history of manic or hypomanic episodes
Cognitive symptoms developed secondary to the onset of depressed mood without spatial disorientation
